claims.text: The baseline phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy has marginal glass-forming ability.
The baseline alloy has limited thermal stability in its amorphous state.
The intervention is addition of 1–5 wt% of a solute having a substantially different atomic size from the main constituents.
The intervention should be tested under cooling conditions near the baseline alloy's critical cooling rate.
Phosphorus content and the remainder of the base-alloy composition should be held constant when comparing modified and baseline alloys.
Keeping the solute within a narrow concentration window can avoid phase separation or secondary crystalline-phase formation.
Atomic-size mismatch from the added solute increases atomic-level disorder.
Atomic-size mismatch increases frustration of local atomic packing.
The increased disorder and packing frustration impede crystalline nucleation and growth.
The size-mismatched solute disrupts ordering tendencies during cooling.
Disruption of ordering increases the kinetic barrier to crystalline nucleation and growth.
The modified alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate for formation of a fully amorphous phase than the solute-free baseline.
The modified alloy will have a higher crystallization onset temperature than the solute-free baseline.
Solute concentrations outside the optimal range may provide no improvement or cause deleterious phase formation.
Cooling conditions substantially different from those near the baseline critical cooling rate may eliminate the improvement or cause deleterious phase formation.
The effect depends on the chemical compatibility of the selected solute with the alloy matrix.
